ch1-coins.title: Find when the two coins always agree
ch1-coins.breaks: Real coins have a hidden answer from the start. Bell pairs do not. You also cannot send a message with them, because each side alone only sees random results.

levels.kid: Which dial settings could make the two coins agree every time?
levels.student: Compare two runs: both cities on the same dial, then the two cities on different dials.

levels.kid: Coins asked the same question give the same answer.
levels.student: When both cities measure in the same basis, their results match every time. Run the flips with both dials on Z, then both on X.

levels.kid: Put both dials on the same letter and flip. Then put them on different letters and flip again.
levels.student: Same basis should give 20 agreements out of 20. Z against X should give about 10, and the 10 change from run to run. The two dial controls are outlined.

levels.kid: Watch the table fill in for both dial settings, one after the other.
levels.student: The page runs 20 flips with Z and Z, then 20 with Z and X. Your own runs stay in the table so you can compare.

levels.kid: Same letters always agree, and different letters agree about half the time, like tossing a fair coin.
levels.student: For the pair (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2, equal bases give equal results every time. Mixed bases give independent 50/50 results.

ch2-links.title: See how many seats a road gets in 30 rounds
ch2-links.breaks: Real attempts take time and hardware. Here a whole round happens in one step.

levels.kid: If each plane lands 8 times out of 10, how many of 6 planes would you expect to land?
levels.student: Expected seats are M times q. Try q = 0.8 and compare the tallest bar with that number.

levels.kid: Each road throws 6 planes, and each plane lands on its own.
levels.student: The seats on one road follow Binomial(6, q), so the tallest bars sit near 6 times q.

levels.kid: Set the slider to 0.8, press Run 30 rounds, and look for the tallest blue bar.
levels.student: At q = 0.8 the exact bars peak at 5 seats (about 0.39) and 6 seats (about 0.26). With only 120 roads in the run, the blue bars wobble around the outlined bars. The slider is outlined.

levels.kid: Watch the page throw 30 rounds of planes and count the seats on each road.
levels.student: The page runs 30 rounds with a fixed seed. Compare each blue bar with the outlined exact bar next to it.

levels.kid: The page ran 30 rounds, and the blue bars land near the outlined ones.
levels.student: Each road's seats follow Binomial(6, q), so with more rounds the blue bars settle onto the outlined bars.

ch3-swap.title: Make cities A and D share a pair they can use
ch3-swap.breaks: The middle city's coins are used up by the join. The end pair is unusable until the phone call arrives.

levels.kid: After B joins its two coins, can A and D use their pair right away?
levels.student: Think about what A and D still do not know about the joined result.

levels.kid: B has to tell A and D how the join turned out.
levels.student: The swap is a Bell-state measurement at B. Its outcome is a classical message that A and D need before they can fix their qubits.

levels.kid: Press Join at B first. Then press Phone A and D.
levels.student: The join is a quantum step at B. The phone call is the classical step, and the arc stays grey until it arrives. The two buttons are outlined.

levels.kid: Watch B join, then watch the message travel to A and D.
levels.student: The page does the join, then sends the classical message from B to both ends. The arc turns usable only after the message arrives.

levels.kid: B joined its two coins, then phoned A and D, and now their pair is usable.
levels.student: A and D needed B's measurement result to correct their qubits, so the pair counted only after the call.

ch4-fidelity.title: Add middle cities until the meter turns red
ch4-fidelity.breaks: The grey is random noise, not a copy, because quantum states cannot be copied. Real swaps also add noise of their own, which this model ignores.

levels.kid: How many middle cities do you think a pair can pass through before it is too washed out?
levels.student: Each swap lowers fidelity. Guess where the meter crosses the line at 0.78.

levels.kid: Every join mixes in a little grey paint.
levels.student: Fidelity falls with each link as F_L = (3 w^L + 1) / 4, so the meter drops fast once there are several links.

levels.kid: Keep pressing Add a middle city and watch the number and the line.
levels.student: With F = 0.95, the path has L links, one more than the middle cities. L = 5 still gives 0.78 or more, and L = 6 gives 0.75. The Add button is outlined.

levels.kid: Watch the page add cities one at a time until the meter turns red.
levels.student: The page adds middle cities until the fidelity drops below 0.78, which happens at 5 middle cities.

levels.kid: Four middle cities are fine, and the fifth one washes the pair out.
levels.student: With F = 0.95, 5 links give 0.781 and 6 links give 0.746, so the limit at f = 0.78 is 4 middle cities.

ch5-rush.title: Serve as many requests as the best possible answer
ch5-rush.breaks: A pair is never cut in half. Each pair travels whole, on a single route.

levels.kid: Which road has the fewest seats, and which request needs it?
levels.student: A request needs its pairs on every link of its route, so look at the weakest link first.

levels.kid: A road can carry only as many pairs as its weakest link.
levels.student: A route's capacity is the smallest seat count along it. When one road is not enough, split the request over roads that share no link.

levels.kid: Draw the request with the fewest options first, and read what the referee says.
levels.student: The shortest roads often take seats another request needs. Try a longer road for a request that has spare choices. The cities of the request you are drawing are outlined.

levels.kid: Watch the best answer drawn in green, with your roads still on screen.
levels.student: The green roads come from the exact solver, qmp.ilp.solve_path, run on this instance in the current mode.

levels.kid: The best answer is drawn for you, and it serves as many requests as any legal answer can.
levels.student: The exact solver tries every legal choice of roads, so no answer under these rules serves more requests.

fig1-walk.title: Predict the walk, then step through it
fig1-walk.breaks: The paper prints alpha 3 as 4/2, but the rule that matches its other values gives 3/2. The chosen path does not change.

levels.kid: From city 7, which neighbour looks best, the one with the better seats-per-step score?
levels.student: Compare the score for city 1 with the score for city 8: the larger fraction wins.

levels.kid: Each neighbour gets a score: seats on the bottleneck, divided by steps to go.
levels.student: alpha_i = min(seats on link k-i, best bottleneck from i to the destination) divided by the hops from i. The walk picks the largest alpha.

levels.kid: City 1 scores 4/3 and city 8 scores 4/2. Which fraction is larger?
levels.student: 4/2 is 2 and 4/3 is about 1.33, so the walk goes to city 8. The two neighbours of city 7 are outlined.

levels.kid: Watch the walk go one step at a time, with the scores shown.
levels.student: Step through the walk in the table of scores. The chosen neighbour is marked at each step.

levels.kid: The walk goes 7, 8, 5, 6 first, then 7, 1, 2, 4, 6 second, and splits the 4 pairs as 2 and 2.
levels.student: Each path has a bottleneck of 4 seats, and the spare-seat rule lets a request use half of them, which is 2 pairs per path.

ch6-dice.title: Guess which plan blocks fewer requests over 30 seeds
ch6-dice.breaks: The 30 seeds are one setup: a 3 by 3 grid and 60 requests. Other sizes or request mixes can give other gaps.

levels.kid: Both plans get the same requests and the same planes. What is left to differ?
levels.student: The only difference is how many roads one request may use.

levels.kid: Splitting a request over two roads gives it more ways to fit.
levels.student: Multipath can use any road that single-path can use, and it can also add roads together, so you would expect its blocking ratio to be lower or equal.

levels.kid: Look at the heuristic pair at the highest q, where blocking is small, and read the paired difference with its error bar.
levels.student: If the 95% interval of the paired difference stays above zero, single-path blocks more by more than chance. The guess box is outlined.

levels.kid: Watch the page draw the chart and the table for all 30 seeds.
levels.student: The page shows the blocking ratio against q with 95% error bars, then the paired differences. Your guess stays on screen.

levels.kid: Multipath blocks fewer requests than single-path for the heuristic pair.
levels.student: The paired difference over 30 seeds is above zero at the 95% level, and both plans saw the same dice.

arena-find.title: Find a window where multipath serves a request that single-path turns away
arena-find.breaks: A window is one round of seat sampling. A request turned away in one window can still be served in a later window, so turned away is not always lost for good.

levels.kid: Which request does the right side serve in this window that the left side does not?
levels.student: Step through the windows and compare the two statuses in each row of the request table.

levels.kid: Splitting lets a request use two thin roads when no single road is wide enough.
levels.student: Single-path needs one road with room for every pair plus a spare seat. Multipath can add up roads that share no link, so it serves some requests the left side turns away.

levels.kid: Tick the box that shows only requests where the two sides differ, then look for a row where the right side says served.
levels.student: Seats are scarcer at a low q, so differences are easier to find there. The filter box is outlined.

levels.kid: Watch the page move to a window where the two sides differ and open that request.
levels.student: The page jumps to the first window where the right side serves a request the left side turns away, ticks the filter, and opens its story. Move the slider to go back.

levels.kid: The page opened a request that the multipath side serves and the single-path side turns away in the same window.
levels.student: Its story names the roads the multipath side used and what the single-path side lacked.

arena-ablate.title: Turn one rule off and predict the change first
arena-ablate.breaks: Switching a rule off shows a precomputed run of the heuristic, not a live recalculation, and it changes only the multipath side. More freedom can still make one later request fail, because an early request takes seats.

levels.kid: If a rule is removed, are requests easier or harder to place?
levels.student: Think about what each rule asks for: spare seats, several roads, or a limit on middle cities.

levels.kid: The spare-seat rule keeps empty seats on every road, so removing it frees seats.
levels.student: With the rule on, one request may use at most half of a link's seats (A21). Without it, a request can take all of them.

levels.kid: Make one guess, more, fewer or the same, and then flip the spare-seat switch.
levels.student: Predict the final count of served requests on the multipath side first. The prediction box and the switches are outlined.

levels.kid: Watch the page turn the spare-seat rule off and list the requests that change.
levels.student: The page flips the switch and lists the requests that become newly served or newly blocked, compared with all rules on.

levels.kid: Turning the spare-seat rule off frees seats, so the multipath side serves the same number of requests or more in the runs shown here.
levels.student: The list under the switches names each request that changed fate.

codelab-c1.title: Challenge 1: beat Lazy Walker
codelab-c1.breaks: The roads from disjoint_paths are not the only way to split a request. Another order or another set of roads may do better or worse on other seeds.

levels.kid: Lazy Walker turns a request away when one road has too few seats. What could it do instead?
levels.student: Look at what choose_paths returns: a list. How many roads can it hold?

levels.kid: Share the request between roads that do not touch, so each road needs only a few seats.
levels.student: Pseudocode: find roads that share no link, widest first. Give each road as many pairs as half its thinnest link allows, until all pairs are placed. If pairs are left over, return an empty list.

levels.kid: The page added a fill-in-the-blank outline at the end of your code, as comments.
levels.student: Fill the blanks: sort by the thinnest link, divide by net.spare, and compare what is left with zero. The Splitter template has the helpers disjoint_paths and thinnest.

levels.kid: Watch the page set your code beside a working answer and mark the lines that differ.
levels.student: Your lines are on the left and the working solution is on the right. A minus marks a line only you have, and a plus marks a line only the solution has.

levels.kid: The page put a working split rule in the editor and ran it.
levels.student: It splits each request over roads with no shared link, widest first, and keeps the paper's spare seat on each road, so it blocks fewer requests than Lazy Walker.

codelab-c2.title: Challenge 2: beat SP-Heu with no illegal answers
codelab-c2.breaks: Winning on 10 seeds does not prove the rule on other grids. A rule can also be legal on these seeds and break a rule on others.

levels.kid: Which rules can make the referee reject an answer?
levels.student: Check the endpoints, the middle-city limit, shared links, the seats on every link, and the total number of pairs.

levels.kid: Only return an answer the referee would accept, and return an empty list when you are unsure.
levels.student: Pseudocode: keep the roads within net.max_middle middle cities. Give each road at most half its thinnest link in pairs. If the pairs do not add up to request.n, return an empty list.

levels.kid: The outline in your editor shows where the limits go.
levels.student: Fill net.max_middle into the road filter and net.spare into the division. The answer is all or nothing, so left must be zero at the end.

levels.kid: Watch the page set your code beside a working answer and mark the lines that differ.
levels.student: Your lines are on the left and the working solution is on the right. A minus marks a line only you have, and a plus marks a line only the solution has.

levels.kid: The page put a legal split rule in the editor and ran it.
levels.student: It keeps roads within the middle-city limit and puts half of each road's thinnest link in pairs, so the referee reports no illegal answers and it blocks fewer requests than SP-Heu.

codelab-c3.title: Challenge 3: beat MP-Heu
codelab-c3.breaks: Using every seat helps here because a blocked request is lost for good. The paper keeps spare seats for a reason, and other setups may reward them.

levels.kid: Your Challenge 2 answer leaves half of every road empty. Is that required?
levels.student: The referee only checks capacity and the physics. Look at net.spare and ask what happens if you divide by 1 instead.

levels.kid: An empty seat helps nobody if the next request is turned away for lack of seats.
levels.student: Pseudocode: give each road as many pairs as its thinnest link allows, not half of it. Keep the rest as before. The extension in the report relaxes the spare seat in a similar way.

levels.kid: The outline marks the one line that changes from Challenge 2.
levels.student: Fill the first blank with 1 so the division keeps no spare seat. The second blank is still zero.

levels.kid: Watch the page set your code beside a working answer and mark the lines that differ.
levels.student: Your lines are on the left and the working solution is on the right. A minus marks a line only you have, and a plus marks a line only the solution has.

levels.kid: The page put a no-spare-seat split rule in the editor and ran it.
levels.student: Each road carries as many pairs as its thinnest link allows, so it blocks fewer requests than MP-Heu.
